result.title: Inherited or Learned? Backdoor Selectivity in Distilled Language Models
result.summary: Distillation is a routine step in building small language models, and a backdoored teacher can pass its backdoor to the student. We study what a student inherits when the backdoor is a rare string that triggers a fixed refusal. Keeping the trigger fixed, we vary only where it appears, at a random word boundary or appended to the instruction, and compare teachers and students on the exact trigger, six control strings and clean inputs. Across Qwen2.5, Llama 3.2 and Gemma 3, with 5% of transfer prompts triggered, randomly inserted triggers become less selective after distillation in all nine teacher-student pipelines, while appended triggers gain selectivity in Qwen and Llama and change little in Gemma. Students trained on the same prompts without a teacher show that much of this is not inherited. Llama and Gemma students learn an appended backdoor from the 150 poisoned examples alone, and only Qwen's 0.5B student needs the teacher. The data also sets where the trigger works. Gemma teachers respond to it anywhere, but their students only when it is appended. Audits should compare teacher and student on the same inputs, probe several trigger positions and include a student trained without the teacher.

AI.brief_summary: 研究蒸馏过程中教师模型的后门（稀有字符串触发固定拒答）如何被学生继承，通过改变触发串出现位置并对比师生输出来区分「继承」与「自行学得」。
AI.relevance_reason: 该工作属纯文本安全与蒸馏审计，关注触发串位置敏感性与拒答行为，未涉及视觉细节保留、latent 推理状态生成或推理期证据使用，位置敏感性线索过弱，难以支撑具体借鉴。
